request: We need a better way to track who is the right person to contact in each country.
system_context: A Government CRM system used in Operations and Country Engagement. The system is the central record of relationships between the organization and its government counterparts: country representatives, ministry contacts, project leads, and mission delegates. It tracks contact details, engagement history, project affiliations, and active missions across ~100 member countries. Users include regional coordinators, project managers, and executive-level staff. Data is sensitive - some contact records carry diplomatic or confidentiality considerations.

content.interpretation: Improve the Government CRM's ability to identify and surface the most appropriate contact person within each country based on user need and context. Users currently find it difficult to determine who to engage when initiating or managing government relationships. The proposal addresses this by adding discovery, filtering, and routing mechanisms that help users quickly find the correct contact given their purpose (project affiliation, geographic region, ministry, contact type) and escalation path.
supplied_facts: The CRM is the central record of relationships with government counterparts across ~100 member countries.
The system tracks contact details, engagement history, project affiliations, and active missions.
Users include regional coordinators, project managers, and executive-level staff.
Data carries diplomatic or confidentiality considerations.
Users report difficulty identifying the right contact person in each country.
included_scope: Enhanced contact discovery and search within the CRM for a given country (by country name, region, or code).
Filtering and ranking contacts by role type (e.g., country representative, ministry contact, project lead, mission delegate), project affiliation, engagement recency, or active mission status.
Display of contact context (history summary, current projects, last engagement date, organizational role) to help users assess appropriateness.
Role-based access controls respected in contact visibility (e.g., confidential contacts shown only to authorized users).
Updated contact record UI to surface metadata that aids selection (e.g., primary vs. backup designations, language, expertise area).
Audit trail for contact selections and routing decisions to support governance and relationship continuity.
excluded_scope: Automated contact recommendation via AI or machine learning (not proposed in this round pending user preference).
Changes to the underlying contact data model or organizational hierarchy structure.
Integration with external contact databases or third-party identity systems.
Workflow automation that removes human judgment from contact selection (users remain responsible for the final choice).
Changes to confidentiality rules or access policy; implementation respects existing policy enforcement.
conditional_scope: If the organization establishes criteria for 'primary' vs. 'secondary' contact designation: the UI will highlight and filter by these designations. The proposal assumes such designation logic will be provided separately or exists but is not yet surfaced in the UI.

If project-to-contact associations are sparse or outdated: filtering by project will have limited utility until data quality is addressed through a separate data governance initiative. The feature will remain functional but may show fewer results.

If regional coordinator preferences for escalation paths are known: the contact ranking can reflect preferred escalation order (e.g., prioritize regional lead over project lead). This requires input on escalation policy.

assumptions.statement: Users can tolerate one additional step (a search or filter action) to find the right contact, compared to today's method.
assumptions.rationale: The request implies dissatisfaction with current discovery speed or ease. Adding a better search interface assumes it will not introduce unacceptable friction; if users need instant pre-selected contacts, a different approach (e.g., dashboard widgets, role-based defaults) might be needed instead.

assumptions.statement: Contact roles (country representative, ministry contact, project lead, mission delegate) are sufficiently distinct and consistently recorded in the CRM to enable reliable filtering.
assumptions.rationale: Filtering by role assumes role data is complete and accurate. If role assignment is inconsistent or missing, filters will fail to surface the intended contact and erode user trust in the feature.

assumptions.statement: The organization has defined rules for which users may access which contacts, and these rules are enforced at the system level today.
assumptions.rationale: The proposal assumes role-based visibility is already in place (as a control measure given data sensitivity). The proposal does not change access rules but must respect them in the improved discovery UI.

assumptions.statement: Users in different roles (e.g., regional coordinator vs. project manager) have overlapping but distinct contact-finding needs, and one unified discovery interface can serve both.
assumptions.rationale: The request uses 'the right person' (singular concept across user types), implying a common problem. If different roles need fundamentally different selection criteria, the solution may need role-specific entry points or views rather than one generic interface.

assumptions.statement: Recording which contact was selected and when is valuable for governance, relationship continuity, and dispute resolution; users will accept the addition of this audit log.
assumptions.rationale: Auditing contact selection supports accountability and helps future users understand why a contact relationship started. If audit overhead is seen as bureaucratic burden, this feature may need to be optional or deferred.

success_criteria: A user can search for contacts in a named country and receive a filtered list (by role, project, mission status, or engagement recency) in under 30 seconds, without contacting support.
At least 80% of contact selections made via the improved interface correspond to the user's stated task or project affiliation (measured by follow-up survey or audit log review of outcomes).
No unauthorized user sees a contact marked as confidential or access-restricted; audit confirms access rules are enforced during contact discovery.
When a user returns to engage the same contact six months later, the CRM shows relevant history and context from prior interactions (to support continuity and avoid redundant introductions).

open_questions.question: What criteria should determine whether one contact is 'more appropriate' than another for a given user in a given country? For example, should a project manager always prefer a project lead contact over a country representative, or does it depend on the nature of the work?
open_questions.impact: This affects the ranking and filtering logic. Without clear criteria, the UI may surface contacts in an order that does not match user intent, reducing perceived usefulness of the feature.

open_questions.question: Are there contacts in the CRM that are restricted from view by certain user roles due to diplomatic sensitivity? If so, what is the current rule set for access, and how should it be integrated into the new contact discovery UI?
open_questions.impact: Implementation of the feature must respect confidentiality without creating loopholes or confusing users who lack access. A mismatch could create security or diplomatic risk.

open_questions.question: Should the improved contact discovery be available through the main CRM interface, a dedicated dashboard widget, mobile app, or some other surface? Does user context (e.g., are they on a country mission or in a planning meeting) affect the preferred interface?
open_questions.impact: The choice of UI surface affects adoption, accessibility, and whether the feature solves the original problem (users may not find it if it is not salient in their workflow).

open_questions.question: Is there a policy or preference for how often contact information should be refreshed (e.g., annual review, on-demand, or tied to mission cycles)? Should the discovery interface surface staleness warnings for contacts not engaged in the past N months?
open_questions.impact: If contact data becomes stale, users may attempt to engage inactive or superseded contacts, damaging relationships. Staleness feedback could mitigate this, but requires data governance rules and user education.

confidence.justification: Grounding: 3/4 — The request and system context clearly establish the problem (difficulty finding the right contact) and the CRM's role as the central relationship record. The proposal is grounded in the stated user types and data sensitivities. One gap: the request does not specify whether the problem is search difficulty, unclear role hierarchy, or lack of context; the proposal assumes it is a discovery/filtering gap. Scope clarity and relevance: 3/4 — Included and excluded scope are defined and coherent. However, two material questions block implementation: (1) the ranking criteria for 'most appropriate' contact are unknown, and (2) access rules for confidential contacts are not detailed in the supplied context, so the proposal cannot fully specify how the feature will enforce them. Assumptions and dependencies: 3/4 — Five material assumptions are explicit (data quality, role consistency, existing access controls, unified interface feasibility, audit acceptance). These are reasonable but not validated; failure of any would require revision. The conditional scope addresses sparse project-to-contact associations and unknown escalation policy. Dependencies on human decisions about ranking criteria and access rules are clearly marked as blocking. Testability: 3/4 — Success criteria are observable (30-second discovery, 80% appropriateness match, access rule enforcement, context retention). Criteria 2 relies on follow-up survey, which is practical but depends on user willingness to provide feedback. Criteria 1 uses a time target (30 seconds); this is proposed based on typical UX expectations, not supplied evidence. Treatment of material concerns: 2/4 — Confidentiality and access control are identified as material and are addressed in conditional scope and assumptions. However, the proposal does not yet specify the detailed mechanism (e.g., will confidential contacts be hidden entirely, shown with redacted fields, or require approval to contact?). Diplomatic sensitivity is acknowledged but not resolved. Recommended cap: Two blocking open questions (ranking criteria, access rules) prevent implementation approval, but the scope is clear enough for human review and decision. Cap of 60 applied. Score: 5 × (3+3+3+3+2) - 10 = 68 after capping.
confidence.main_uncertainty: What explicit criteria define the 'right' contact for a given user and task, and how should these be surfaced and ranked in the UI? The request assumes a common understanding of contact appropriateness, but the CRM serves multiple user roles (regional coordinators, project managers, executives) with potentially different priorities. A second close uncertainty is the precise treatment of access-restricted or diplomatically sensitive contacts in the discovery workflow — whether they are excluded, shown with warnings, or require prior authorization to view. Both require human input from stakeholders (leadership or business analysts) and will materially affect the scope and UX design once clarified.

accepted_points: The request identifies a genuine operational problem: users in a Government CRM serving ~100 countries report difficulty identifying the correct contact person.

The proposed scope (enhanced discovery, filtering, ranking, context display, access control respect, audit trail) is coherent and addresses the stated problem through improved information access rather than automated decision-making.
The exclusion of AI/ML recommendation, data model changes, and workflow automation that removes human judgment is defensible and keeps the scope bounded.

The five explicit assumptions (user tolerance for extra steps, role consistency, existing access controls, unified interface feasibility, audit acceptance) are material and reasonable to state upfront.

The conditional scope appropriately flags dependencies on primary/secondary designation logic, project-to-contact data quality, and escalation policy—none of which are supplied in the current context but are plausible to address separately.
The success criteria are testable: 30-second discovery time, 80% appropriateness match via survey/audit, access rule enforcement verification, and context retention are all observable.
The proposal correctly identifies that implementation depends on human decisions about ranking criteria and access rule details, and marks these as blocking.

challenges.concern: The proposal states contacts should be filtered and ranked by role, project affiliation, engagement recency, and mission status, but does not specify the ranking algorithm or rules. For example: should a project manager always prefer a project lead contact over a country representative, or does it depend on task type? Should a recently inactive but historically strong contact be ranked below a recently active but less relevant one? Without explicit ranking rules, the UI may surface contacts in an order that does not match user intent, reducing perceived usefulness and trust in the feature.
challenges.resolution_needed: Provide or obtain from stakeholders explicit criteria for determining contact appropriateness and ranking order by user role or task type. For example: a decision matrix showing which contact roles are preferred for different engagement types (policy negotiation, project delivery, crisis escalation, routine liaison), or a rule set for how recency trades off against historical relevance. This may require input from regional coordinators, project managers, or leadership.

challenges.target: Access control and confidentiality enforcement in contact discovery
challenges.concern: The proposal acknowledges that some contacts carry diplomatic or confidentiality restrictions and that role-based access controls must be respected, but does not specify the mechanism. Should access-restricted contacts be hidden entirely from unauthorized users, shown with redacted fields, shown with a 'contact support' call-to-action, or excluded from filters? An incorrect choice could create a security loophole (unauthorized users gain awareness of restricted contacts) or a usability trap (users see a contact in search results but cannot access it, without clear explanation). The supplied system context confirms data sensitivity but does not detail the current access rule set.
challenges.resolution_needed: Clarify the current access control rules for contact records (which roles can see which contact categories, and under what conditions). Then specify how the new discovery UI will enforce these rules: will restricted contacts be filtered out of results for unauthorized users, or shown with restricted access indicators? Who approves access to restricted contacts, and should the discovery flow provide a path for requesting access?

challenges.target: Definition of 'the right person' across user roles
challenges.concern: The proposal assumes 'the right person' is a concept that applies uniformly to regional coordinators, project managers, and executive-level staff, and that one unified discovery interface can serve all. However, these roles likely have different contact-finding priorities: a project manager may prioritize contacts for a specific project, a regional coordinator may prioritize by geography and escalation path, and an executive may prioritize strategic relationships. If contact selection criteria differ materially by role, a single unified interface may produce confusing or unhelpful results for some users.
challenges.resolution_needed: Confirm whether different user roles have overlapping or distinct contact selection criteria. If distinct, clarify whether the proposal should include role-specific filtering/ranking views, separate entry points to the discovery feature, or a unified interface with role-aware defaults. If overlapping with minor differences, specify how role context should influence ranking.

challenges.target: Data quality assumptions for role and project assignment
challenges.concern: The proposal assumes role data (country representative, ministry contact, project lead, mission delegate) is sufficiently complete and consistently recorded to enable reliable filtering. If role assignment is sparse, missing, or inconsistent across the CRM, filtering by role will surface incomplete or misleading results, eroding user trust. Similarly, filtering by project affiliation assumes project-to-contact associations are current and comprehensive. The proposal flags project data quality as a conditional dependency, but does not assess whether role data quality meets the baseline assumption.
challenges.resolution_needed: Confirm the current state of role data completeness in the CRM (e.g., what percentage of contacts have a role designation, how consistent is the role taxonomy). If data quality gaps exist, specify whether the proposal should proceed with degraded filtering capability (showing a warning to users), include a data remediation step as a prerequisite, or defer the feature pending data cleanup. This affects the feasibility of success criterion 2 (80% appropriateness match).

challenges.concern: The proposal defines success as 'at least 80% of contact selections made via the improved interface correspond to the user's stated task or project affiliation,' measured by follow-up survey or audit log review. This is testable in principle, but depends on two unknowns: (1) what constitutes a 'match' between contact and task (which relates to C1, ranking criteria), and (2) how survey response bias will be controlled (users who are satisfied may be more likely to respond, inflating the match rate). The criterion is also proposed without evidence that 80% is a realistic or acceptable threshold.
challenges.resolution_needed: Clarify what 'appropriateness' means operationally (does the contact's role align with the task type? Is there an existing project relationship? Did the engagement achieve its stated outcome?). Propose a measurement method that accounts for response bias (e.g., random sampling, outcome auditing rather than survey). Justify the 80% target or revise to a lower baseline (e.g., 70%) if 80% is speculative.

challenges.concern: The proposal includes an audit trail for contact selections and routing decisions to support governance and relationship continuity. However, it does not specify what data will be recorded (user identity, timestamp, contact selected, alternative contacts shown?, task context?), how long audit records will be retained, who can access them, or how they will be used. Overrecording could create privacy friction or compliance burden; underrecording could limit the audit trail's usefulness for governance. Unclear retention or access policies could create disputes if a contact relationship is later questioned.
challenges.resolution_needed: Specify the audit trail schema (what fields will be recorded), retention period, and access controls. Confirm that recording user selection choices is acceptable under the organization's privacy or data governance policy. If audit records themselves are sensitive, specify how they will be protected.

open_questions.question: What explicit criteria or decision rules should govern which contact is 'most appropriate' for a given user task or engagement type? Should this be expressed as a rank order (e.g., 'prefer project lead > country representative > ministry contact'), a task-dependent matrix (e.g., 'for policy negotiation, prefer ministry contact; for project delivery, prefer project lead'), or a user-role-specific preference?
open_questions.impact: This directly affects the ranking algorithm and UI design. Without clear criteria, the feature may not surface the contacts users actually need, reducing adoption and usefulness. This is the core gap preventing implementation.

open_questions.question: What is the current set of access control rules governing contact visibility (i.e., which user roles or groups can view which categories of contacts, and under what circumstances)? How should access-restricted contacts be treated in the new discovery UI—hidden entirely, shown with access warnings, or excluded from certain filter results?
open_questions.impact: The feature must respect existing access policy to avoid security or diplomatic risk. Unclear rules leave the implementation open to loopholes or confusion. This is a prerequisite for finalizing the confidentiality and access control design.

open_questions.question: Do regional coordinators, project managers, and executive-level staff have sufficiently overlapping contact selection criteria that a single unified discovery interface will serve all roles well? Or should the feature include role-specific views, entry points, or ranking defaults?
open_questions.impact: If roles have materially different needs, a one-size-fits-all interface may confuse or frustrate some users. Role-awareness could improve adoption but adds complexity. This affects the overall UX architecture.

open_questions.question: What is the current state of data quality for contact role assignments and project-to-contact associations in the CRM? If these data are sparse or inconsistent, should the feature proceed with degraded filtering capability, include a data remediation step, or be deferred?
open_questions.impact: Poor data quality will undermine the filtering feature's usefulness and erode user trust. This affects the feasibility of achieving the 80% appropriateness success criterion.

open_questions.question: How should the success criterion 'at least 80% of contact selections correspond to the user's stated task' be measured operationally, and how was the 80% target justified? Should measurement rely on follow-up survey, audit log analysis of outcome, or other method?
open_questions.impact: Vague measurement methods or unjustified thresholds make it difficult to assess whether the feature is actually working as intended post-launch. Clarity here supports effective governance and potential iteration.

open_questions.question: Should the improved contact discovery be surfaced in the main CRM interface, as a dedicated dashboard widget, via mobile app, or in some other form? Does the choice depend on whether users are in-country on a mission, in-office planning, or remote?
open_questions.impact: Feature discoverability and accessibility affect adoption. If the discovery interface is not salient in users' typical workflows, they may not use it and revert to old (inefficient) contact-finding methods.

content.assessment_reason: The proposal provides clear scope and explicit assumptions suitable for human review, but contains three material blockers that prevent agreement on implementation: (1) ranking criteria for contact appropriateness are undefined, preventing the feature from being built without guesswork; (2) access control rules for confidential contacts are not detailed, leaving a security and usability gap; (3) the assumption that a single unified interface serves all user roles is not validated and may be incorrect. These are not questions about external research or policy verification—they are questions about the organization's own contact-finding practices and access policies, which stakeholders can answer. Another exchange with the Proposer's clarification or defense of these points, or request for guidance from regional/project leadership, can resolve them. Success criteria 1 and 4 are sound; C4, C5, and C6 are refinements that improve rigor but are not implementation blockers if addressed through governance or post-launch measurement.
content.next_exchange: The Proposer should address the three blocking challenges (C1, C2, C3) by either: (1) providing or proposing explicit ranking criteria and rules for contact appropriateness, with justification or a request for stakeholder input; (2) clarifying whether current access control rules are documented and how they should be enforced in the discovery UI; and (3) validating or revising the assumption that a unified interface serves all user roles. For each blocker, the Proposer should state whether this information is available from organizational context not yet shared, or whether human decision-making by a named group (e.g., regional coordinators, product leadership) is needed before design can proceed. This will determine whether the scope can move to a conditional agreement pending those decisions, or whether further research is required.

confidence.justification: Grounding: 3/4 — The proposal is grounded in the stated problem (users report difficulty finding contacts) and the CRM's established role. The interpretation of the problem as a discovery/filtering gap is reasonable but not explicitly confirmed in the original request, which uses the vaguer phrase 'better way to track.' Scope clarity and relevance: 3/4 — Included and excluded scope are well-defined and coherent. However, two material gaps prevent full clarity: (a) ranking criteria for contact appropriateness are undefined, and (b) access control enforcement mechanism is not detailed. Both affect the feature's design and feasibility. Assumptions and dependencies: 3/4 — Five material assumptions are explicit and stated with rationales. They are reasonable but not yet validated; failure of any would require revision. Testability: 3/4 — Success criteria are observable and mostly evidence-based, with the exception that the 80% appropriateness threshold and the 30-second time target are proposed without external evidence. Treatment of material concerns: 2/4 — Confidentiality and access control are identified as concerns and are addressed at a high level (respect existing rules, show context, include audit trail). However, the proposal does not yet specify how these will be enforced in the discovery UI or what the access rules actually are. This leaves a material gap that could affect both security and usability. No cap is applied: the three blocking open questions (C1, C2, C3) prevent implementation approval, but the scope is clear enough for human review and a second deliberation round can resolve them. Score calculated as 5 × (3+3+3+3+2) = 70; no cap.
confidence.main_uncertainty: The most material unresolved issue is the definition of contact appropriateness and ranking criteria (C1). The request assumes 'the right person' is a coherent concept, but the proposal does not articulate what makes one contact 'righter' than another for a given user and task. This requires either explicit business rules (which may exist but are not documented), a user research or stakeholder input process to derive them, or a decision to defer ranking and surface undifferentiated search results (a lower-value feature). The second close uncertainty is how access-restricted contacts will be treated in discovery (C2)—whether hidden, shown with redacted fields, or shown with access-request workflows. Both are organizational policy/design decisions, not information gaps, and can be resolved by the Proposer in the next round through stakeholder consultation or clarification of existing practices.

Until these criteria are articulated, the feature will surface filtered results in a neutral order (e.g., alphabetical or by recency), and users will apply judgment to select the appropriate contact.

If project-to-contact associations are sparse or outdated: filtering by project will have limited utility until data quality is addressed through a separate data governance initiative. The feature will remain functional but may show fewer results.

The contact discovery feature is actively used by at least 60% of regional coordinators and project managers within the first quarter of launch, as measured by system telemetry.

At least 70% of contact selections made via the improved interface correspond to the user's stated task, project affiliation, or stated engagement purpose, as measured by audit log review of outcomes or follow-up validation conducted by regional coordinators.
When a user returns to engage the same contact six months later, the CRM shows relevant history and context from prior interactions (to support continuity and avoid redundant introductions).
No unauthorized user sees a contact marked as confidential or access-restricted in search results or filter suggestions; access control enforcement is validated quarterly through audit log review.

responses.rationale: The Critic is correct that ranking criteria are undefined and are essential to the feature's usefulness. I revise the proposal to address this by moving contact ranking to conditional scope: until explicit ranking criteria are established by the organization, the feature will surface filtered results in a neutral order (e.g., alphabetical or by recency). Users will apply judgment to select the appropriate contact. This is a lower-value initial release but operationally sound and prevents the feature from ranking contacts incorrectly. I propose that ranking rules be established through a subsequent discovery process with regional coordinators, project managers, and leadership, who can articulate task-type-specific preferences (e.g., 'for policy negotiation prefer ministry contact; for project delivery prefer project lead'). Alternatively, the organization may decide to gather these criteria during an initial pilot. This avoids guesswork and ensures ranking serves actual user needs.

The Critic correctly identifies that the proposal acknowledges access control requirements but does not specify the enforcement mechanism. I revise the proposal to add explicit conditional scope: once the access control rule set is documented, the discovery UI will enforce these rules by: (1) filtering access-restricted contacts from view for unauthorized users; (2) displaying a 'contact support for access' message when an unauthorized user encounters a restriction; (3) maintaining an audit record of access attempts; and (4) ensuring restricted contacts do not appear in search results, filter suggestions, or rankings for users without authorization. This mechanism prevents security loopholes (unauthorized awareness of restricted contacts) and provides clarity to users. I make this approach conditional on the access control rules being documented and provided to the implementation team. Until then, the feature will respect the current system-level access enforcement but will not add new access control logic.

The Critic raises a valid concern: regional coordinators, project managers, and executives may have materially different contact selection criteria, and a single unified interface may not serve all roles well. I revise the assumption (A4) to acknowledge this explicitly and propose that the unified interface include role-aware filtering and context (e.g., regional coordinators see a 'region' and 'escalation path' filter; project managers see a 'project affiliation' and 'delivery stage' filter). However, I recognize that this may not be sufficient if roles have incompatible needs. I propose that the organization validate this assumption through stakeholder consultation with representatives from each user role before final design. If the validation shows that roles need fundamentally different views or entry points, the scope can be revised to include role-specific discovery workflows. For the current proposal, the unified interface with role-aware defaults is defensible as a starting point, but requires stakeholder sign-off on role-specific priorities to proceed to design.

open_questions.question: What explicit ranking or prioritization criteria should govern contact appropriateness for different engagement types (e.g., policy negotiation, project delivery, crisis escalation, routine liaison)? Should these be expressed as role-aware preferences, task-type matrices, or escalation hierarchies?
open_questions.impact: Ranking criteria determine whether the feature surfaces contacts in the order users need. Without criteria, the feature provides search and filtering (useful) but not intelligent ranking (more useful). This affects perceived value and adoption. If criteria cannot be articulated, the feature will proceed with neutral ordering and recommend ranking be addressed in a later iteration based on pilot feedback.

open_questions.question: What is the current, documented set of access control rules governing contact visibility in the CRM (i.e., which user roles or groups can view which categories of contacts, and under what circumstances)? How are these rules currently enforced at the system level?
open_questions.impact: The feature must respect existing access policy to avoid security or diplomatic risk. The implementation team requires documentation of these rules to design the access enforcement mechanism in the discovery UI. Without documented rules, implementation cannot proceed with confidence.

open_questions.question: Do regional coordinators, project managers, and executive-level staff have sufficiently overlapping contact selection priorities that a single unified discovery interface (with role-aware filtering and defaults) will serve all adequately? Or do different roles require materially distinct selection criteria that would benefit from separate entry points or workflows?
open_questions.impact: If roles have overlapping priorities, a unified interface with role-aware filtering is efficient. If roles have incompatible priorities, separate workflows may be needed, affecting scope and complexity. This requires stakeholder validation with representatives from each user role.

open_questions.question: What is the current state of data quality for contact role assignments in the CRM (e.g., what percentage of contacts have a role designation, and how consistent is the role taxonomy across countries and regions)? If data quality is below 70%, should the feature proceed with a data remediation requirement, proceed with degraded filtering capability and a warning banner, or be deferred?
open_questions.impact: Poor role data quality will undermine filtering reliability and erode user trust. This affects feasibility of the success criteria around contact appropriateness and discovery speed. A baseline assessment is needed before feature launch.

open_questions.question: Should the improved contact discovery be surfaced in the main CRM interface, a dedicated dashboard widget, a mobile app, or another surface? Does user context (e.g., in-country mission vs. in-office planning) affect the preferred interface?
open_questions.impact: Feature discoverability affects adoption. If the discovery interface is not salient in users' workflows, they may not use it. This is a lower-priority decision but affects go-to-market success.

open_questions.question: What audit data should be recorded for contact selections (e.g., user identity, timestamp, contact selected, alternative contacts shown, task context)? How long should audit records be retained, and who should have access to them for governance purposes?
open_questions.impact: Audit trail supports governance and relationship continuity. However, overrecording creates privacy friction; underrecording limits usefulness. Clarity on schema, retention, and access prevents disputes and ensures compliance with data governance policy.

confidence.justification: Grounding: 3/4 — The proposal remains grounded in the stated problem (users report difficulty finding contacts) and the CRM's established role. The interpretation is reasonable but not explicitly confirmed as the root cause; the original request uses the vaguer phrase 'better way to track,' which could also be addressed by roster/list improvements or automated routing. Scope clarity and relevance: 3/4 — Included and excluded scope are well-defined and coherent. The revisions to conditional scope (neutral ranking until criteria are established, access enforcement conditional on documented rules) clarify material dependencies. One gap remains: role-specific selection priorities are flagged as requiring stakeholder validation but are not yet validated. Assumptions and dependencies: 3/4 — Five material assumptions are explicit, including the revised A4 acknowledging that unified interface feasibility depends on role-priority overlap (which requires validation). Conditional scope now explicitly addresses ranking deferral and access control enforcement conditions, making dependencies clear. Testability: 3/4 — Success criteria are observable. Criteria 2 and 3 are revised: adoption is measured by system telemetry (concrete); appropriateness match is lowered to 70% (more realistic than 80% and avoids unsupported targets) and is measured by audit log or validation by regional coordinators (more robust than survey alone). Criteria 1 (30-second search) and 4 (context retention) remain sound. Criteria 5 (access control verification) is added and is auditable. Treatment of material concerns: 3/4 — Confidentiality and access control are now moved from assumption to conditional scope and are addressed with an explicit mechanism (filtering, messaging, audit) contingent on documented access control rules. Ranking criteria are acknowledged as a dependency that will be deferred until stakeholder input is obtained or pilot feedback is available. This is more transparent than defending an undefined mechanism. The proposal no longer claims to solve ranking without input; instead, it provides search and filtering (core value) and treats ranking as a later enhancement. No cap is applied. The three blocking challenges are now addressed: C1 is revised (ranking deferred to neutral order pending criteria); C2 is revised (access control conditional on documented rules); C3 is revised (unified interface proposed with role-awareness, but flagged for stakeholder validation). The feature can proceed with stakeholder decisions on access control rules and role priorities. Score: 5 × (3+3+3+3+3) = 75; adjusted to 72 to reflect that two key dependencies (access control rules, role-priority validation) remain external to the proposal but are now explicit and actionable.
confidence.main_uncertainty: The most material unresolved issue is whether documented access control rules exist and can be provided to inform the discovery UI's enforcement mechanism (C2). If access rules are not documented or are inconsistently applied, the feature cannot safely enforce them without creating security or usability gaps. This is an organizational policy/governance question, not an information gap, and requires a named stakeholder (likely the CRM administration or security team) to clarify within the next 1–2 weeks before detailed design begins. A secondary uncertainty is whether role-specific contact selection priorities are sufficiently similar that a single unified interface will serve all user roles adequately (C3). This requires validation through interviews or workshops with regional coordinators, project managers, and 1–2 executives. If these conversations reveal incompatible priorities, the scope would need to include role-specific filtering defaults or separate entry points. These two decisions are prerequisites for design; they do not block the current proposal, which is now conditionally sound pending their resolution.
